findings.title: Error-level logging used for routine, non-error cleanup events, including full ID list dumps
findings.body: In CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags, r.log.Error(...) is called unconditionally on every successful batch iteration (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), even though the preceding error checks already returned on actual errors (so `err` logged here is always nil). This mislabels normal operation as an error, which will pollute error logs/alerts and error-rate metrics/dashboards that key off log severity. Additionally, the full `ids` slice (which can be tens of thousands of entries given AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize can be configured up to 32767+ as shown in the new test) is serialized into every log line, which is expensive and will bloat log storage/throughput when cleanup runs frequently (especially now that the cleanup job interval was reduced to 1 minute). These should be Debug level and should not dump entire ID arrays.

findings.title: Unexplained change of cleanup job ticker interval from 10 minutes to 1 minute affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotations
findings.body: The ticker driving CleanUpService.Run was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is a 10x increase in the frequency of the entire cleanup job list (temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, user invites, stale short URLs, stale query history) — not just the annotation cleanup logic that this PR is meant to fix. This change is not mentioned in the PR description, has no accompanying rationale, and no test coverage. Running all of these jobs 10x more often increases database load system-wide and could introduce new contention/performance issues, which seems inconsistent with a PR whose stated goal is reducing lock contention.

findings.title: O(n^2) string concatenation when building literal ID list for SQLite large-batch delete
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size over 999, the code builds the IN(...) literal values by repeatedly doing `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop (lines ~609-612). Each iteration reallocates and copies the growing string, making this O(n^2) in the number of IDs. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands (as exercised by the new test with batch size 32767), this results in unnecessary CPU and memory overhead compared to using a strings.Builder or similar amortized approach.

findings.title: Test name references SQLite >= 3.32.0 behavior but code uses the conservative pre-3.32.0 parameter limit
findings.body: The new test case is named "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0", implying it targets SQLite's newer default limit of 32766. However, the production code's sqliteParameterLimit constant (xorm_store.go) is hardcoded to 999 — the pre-3.32.0 default — so the literal-value workaround is triggered for any batch size above 999, regardless of SQLite version. The test therefore does not actually validate behavior specific to the 3.32.0 threshold; it only exercises the already-conservative workaround path, making the test name misleading about what scenario is being verified.

findings.title: No test demonstrates or guards against the MySQL deadlock the PR is intended to fix
findings.body: The PR's entire motivation is a MySQL-specific deadlock between annotation cleanup and concurrent inserts (grafana/grafana#64979), caused by a single DELETE-with-subquery statement. The added/changed tests (cleanup_test.go) only run against the test DB (typically SQLite) and verify functional correctness of batched deletion, not the concurrency/deadlock behavior that motivated the change. There is no test (e.g., a concurrent-insert-during-cleanup scenario) that would catch a regression back to the deadlocking pattern or validate that the fix actually avoids it under contention.
